paragraphs.text: The appellant, XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Tunisia, is appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), which rejected his claim for refugee protection by finding that he is neither a "Convention refugee" nor a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

In the memorandum of appeal, counsel for the appellant is asking the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to allow the appeal, set aside the RPD determination, determine that the appellant is a person in need of protection or refer the matter to the RPD for re-determination of the refugee protection claim by a different member.1

The memorandum indicates that [translation] "evidence was presented in accordance with the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA for this appeal,"2 yet no new evidence or submission was included with the appellant's record. In this context, I find that no new evidence was submitted in support of this appeal.
In the memorandum, the appellant is requesting that a hearing be held and requires the services of an interpreter so that his spouse can testify.3 DETERMINATION OF THE APPEAL

Pursuant to subsection 111(1) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD, namely, that XXXX XXXX is neither a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA nor a "person in need of protection" under section 97 of the IRPA.
The appeal is dismissed.

The refugee protection claimant is a citizen of Tunisia and a Muslim. He came to Canada as a visitor on XXXX XXXX, 2014. He made a refugee protection claim on May 4, 2015. He alleges a well-founded fear of persecution and a risk to his life by reason of his marriage to a Catholic woman in XXXX 2015 and his attending Catholic churches.

In his Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), he alleges that he began dating an XXXX woman of the Catholic faith. He agreed to convert to Christianity in order to marry his wife. The claimant's parents were informed of his marriage and that he was going to church in Canada.
His family in Tunisia considers him a shame on the family. He alleges that, in Tunisia, death awaits anyone who changes religion. Impugned decision

On July 27, 2015, the RPD rejected the refugee protection claim, finding that [translation] "the claimant was not credible and his testimony was not trustworthy with regard to the central elements of the claim." The RPD noted several omissions in the BOC Form, and inconsistencies and implausibilities in the evidence. In short, the RPD [translation] "believes that the claimant did not convert to Catholicism and did not demonstrate that he intended to do so."4 In addition, the panel draws a negative inference from the claimant's lack of effort to corroborate his testimony on his willingness to convert to Catholicism.

The RPD noted that the documentary evidence indicates that there is nothing prohibiting Muslims from marrying non-Muslims, and that there are many mixed couples in Tunisia. According to the RPD, the evidence does not allow for the conclusion that Muslims married to Christians are systematically persecuted in Tunisia. GROUNDS FOR APPEAL AND REMEDY SOUGHT Appellant's allegations
The appellant submits that the RPD erred by rejecting his refugee protection claim.
The appellant is relying on Maldonado5 and submits that sworn testimony is presumed to be true, unless there is a valid reason to doubt its truthfulness.

He also cited the Federal Court of Appeal decision in Giron,6 which advises caution when making adverse findings based on implausibilities because refugee protection claimants come from diverse cultures and "actions which might appear implausible if judged by Canadian standards might be plausible when considered within the context of the claimant's social and cultural background." Holding a hearing
The claimant is invoking the provisions of subsection 110(6) of the IRPA, and is asking to be heard before the RAD and to call his wife as a witness.

In Singh,7 the Federal Court of Appeal reiterated the principle that the RAD proceed without holding a hearing. According to the Court, this principle "is subject to an exception only where the documentary evidence '(a) [...] raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal; (b) [...] is central to the decision with respect to the refugee protection claim; and (c) [...] if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.'"
In this case, the appellant submitted no new evidence in support of his appeal. Therefore, the RAD cannot hold a hearing.

In Huruglica,8 the Federal Court of Appeal ruled on the issue of whether it was reasonable for the RAD, when credibility was not an issue, to examine the findings of fact, mixed fact and law by using the reasonableness standard.

Interpreting the statutory provisions and making a passing reference to Parliament's intention in implementing the RAD, Justice Gauthier notes: [98] The RAD was essentially viewed as the safety net that would catch all mistakes made by the RPD, be it on the law or the facts.

Parliament's intention must be determined by referring first to the statute, specifically to sections 110 and 111 of the IRPA, about which the Court of Appeal indicates: [59] ... Paragraph 111(2)(a) does not distinguish between errors of law, fact or mixed fact and law. It simply requires that the decision of the RPD be "wrong in law, in fact or in mixed fact and law" (in French: "erronée en droit, en fait ou en droit et en fait"). [64] The ordinary meaning of the word "wrong" is "not correct or true", "incorrect", "mistaken": The Oxford English Dictionary, 3d ed., s.v. "wrong". The French version "erronée" has the exact same ordinary meaning, that is, "fausse", "incorrecte", "inexacte", "mal fondée": Le nouveau petit Robert, 2006, s.v. "erroné". This wording definitively points to the standard of correctness. In addition, the legislator's intent to use the word "wrong" in its ordinary meaning is, in my view, supported by the legislative history, to which I will refer later.

According to the Court, the legislative text recognizes: [70] ... that there may be cases where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage over the RAD in making findings of fact or mixed fact and law, because they require an assessment of the credibility or weight to be given to the oral evidence it hears. It further indicates that although the RAD should sometimes exercise a degree of restraint before substituting its own determination, the issue of whether the circumstances warrant such restraint ought to be addressed on a case-by-case basis. In each case, the RAD ought to determine whether the RPD truly benefited from an advantageous position, and if so, whether the RAD can nevertheless make a final decision in respect of the refugee claim.

After noting examples of possible situations, the Court of Appeal mentions that the level of deference "owed in each case" varies and finds: [78] At this stage of my analysis, I find that the role of the RAD is to intervene when the RPD is wrong in law, in fact or in fact and law. This translates into an application of the correctness standard of review. If there is an error, the RAD can still confirm the decision of the RPD on another basis. It can also set it aside, substituting its own determination of the claim, unless it is satisfied that it cannot do either without hearing the evidence presented to the RPD: paragraph 111(2)(b) of the IRPA.

In response to the question reformulated by the Court of Appeal, the Honourable Justice Gauthier holds: [103] ... with respect to findings of fact (and mixed fact and law) such as the one involved here, which raised no issue of credibility of oral evidence, the RAD is to review RPD decisions applying the correctness standard. Thus, after carefully considering the RPD decision, the RAD carries out its own analysis of the record to determine whether, as submitted by the appellant, the RPD erred. Having done this, the RAD is to provide a final determination, either by confirming the RPD decision or setting it aside and substituting its own determination of the merits of the refugee claim. It is only when the RAD is of the opinion that it cannot provide such a final determination without hearing the oral evidence presented to the RPD that the matter can be referred back to the RPD for redetermination.

Considering what the Court of Appeal states, I will conduct an independent analysis of the evidence in order to formulate my own opinion on this refugee protection claim and to determine whether the decision rendered is correct. If an error of fact, of law or of mixed fact and law has been made, I will intervene through the remedies set out in the IRPA.

Before the RPD, the determinative issue was the appellant's credibility. Generally, the RPD is in a more privileged position than the RAD because it has the advantage of seeing and hearing the refugee protection claimants and witnesses.9 In this case, the RAD will not have this privilege because it will not hold a hearing. However, I must conduct an independent assessment of the evidence to determine whether the decision rendered is correct. If an error of fact, of law or of mixed fact and law has been made, I will have to intervene through a method set out in the IRPA.

I reviewed all the evidence in order to formulate my own opinion on this refugee protection claim. Furthermore, I note that the appellant's memorandum is not very eloquent regarding the errors made by the RPD in the assessment of his refugee protection claim. After considering the few arguments presented and the analysis of the evidence, it is my opinion that the RPD rendered the correct decision. My reasons are as follows.

The presumption of truthfulness mentioned in Maldonado is not unchallengeable and a claimant's lack of credibility is sufficient to rebut it. In addition, although some evidence may not be sufficient when taken individually, the accumulation of contradictions or omissions may serve as a basis for a negative credibility finding,10 which is true in this case. Omissions in the BOC Form

One factor that the RPD found undermined the appellant's credibility was the omission in the BOC Form of several elements central to his refugee protection claim. In particular, the appellant testified that, in XXXX 2015, his brother and his cousin had threatened to torture him because he had married a Catholic and was attending a Catholic church. However, the claimant did not mention these threats in his BOC Form. His explanation that he had put general information in his BOC Form without providing details was deemed insufficient by the RPD.

The appellant argued that the RPD erred in drawing a negative inference from that omission. He stated that he [translation] "testified in his written form that he feared his family, implying that they had threatened him and should not in any way undermine his credibility. It was a logical consequence of leaving Islam to join another religion."11 With due respect for the argument presented, I cannot accept it.

A long line of case law has established that the Board can base its negative credibility findings on the omissions and inconsistencies that it notes regarding the important facts alleged in the notes taken at the point of entry, in the Personal Information Form and in the oral testimony.12

The RPD was justified in drawing a negative inference from the fact that the claimant failed to mention those threats in the BOC Form and to give some details. In fact, question 2(a) of the BOC Form requires claimants to explain in detail what happened to them and when.13 Likewise, the appellant failed to indicate in the BOC Form that his cousin is a tough man, that he is a member of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX an XXXXgroupXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in Tunisia. As the RPD noted, these are not trivial facts; they relate to the threats that form the basis of his fear.

The RPD drew a negative inference from the fact that the claimant also failed to indicate in the BOC Form that his family marginalized him in Tunisia because he did not follow the precepts of Islam; he drank alcohol, did not go to the mosque regularly and did not observe Ramadan in XXXX. The omission of these aspects in the BOC Form, about which he testified, undermined his credibility, especially since the claimant stated in the BOC Form that he did not have any problems in Tunisia due to his religion. Contradictions

The RPD noted a contradiction that I find important. The claimant stated in the BOC Form that he attended XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX church with his wife. Yet, at the hearing, he stated that he went without her. This is not a trivial contradiction and tends to support serious doubt when he states he attends a Christian church.

The appellant also contradicted himself about how frequently he attended mass and the language in which it was celebrated. At the hearing, he stated first that he attended mass four or five times on XXXX XXXXnd that the mass was in XXXX. When confronted with the fact that mass at the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX is on XXXX and that it is celebrated in XXXX and in XXXX, the claimant changed his testimony and answered that he attended two churches. Again, the facts are not trivial; his attending a Christian church is at the heart of his problems. The contradictions in his testimony tend to support serious doubt.

In the credibility assessment, and to find that [translation] "the panel believes that the claimant did not convert to Catholicism and did not demonstrate that he intended to do so,"14 the RPD also considered the following factors. The claimant did not take catechism classes and did not register for catechism classes. He is unable to name one of the sacraments of the Catholic religion. This may seem unimportant, but in this case, the appellant claims to have consulted the parish priest about a possible baptism and, furthermore, he did not know the name of the priest with whom he had discussed this. Lack of corroboration of the claimant's testimony

A claimant's testimony cannot be discredited simply because it is not corroborated by the documentary evidence.15 However, the Board may take account of the absence of corroborative evidence in circumstances where one would expect it to exist.16 In this case, the RPD, due to an accumulation of problems related to the claimant's statements, had serious doubts about his allegations. In my opinion, it was justified in this context to draw a negative inference from the fact that the appellant's wife did not corroborate the claimant's testimony either by testifying directly or by submitting an affidavit. The RPD noted that the appellant's lack of effort to obtain an affidavit from his wife undermined his credibility. In my opinion, it was an element that the RPD could have expected and, in the context of this case, the RPD was justified to consider that element. Implausibility

The RPD drew a negative inference from the implausibility that a conservative Catholic family had allowed their daughter to marry a Muslim man before he converted, when it was a condition of their accepting the union.

It is important to be cautious when finding that a refugee protection claimant is not credible on the basis of the implausibility of an alleged fact. In Subramaniyathas,17 the Federal Court states: "In contrast to credibility findings based on inconsistencies, contradictions or evasions, credibility findings based on implausibility may only be made in the clearest of cases." I am of the opinion that this finding is not determinative in this case.
As noted by the RPD, it is curious that the refugee protection claimant stated that he had renounced Islam but that he still presents himself as Muslim.

For these reasons, it is my opinion that the RPD rendered the correct decision in this case; the appellant did not establish that the decision is not based on the evidence or that the RPD committed an error in fact, in law or in mixed fact and law. In light of the evidence in the record, I would have rendered the same decision.

For these reasons, I confirm the determination of the RPD, namely, that XXXX XXXX is neither a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA nor a "person in need of protection" under section 97 of the IRPA.

The appeal is dismissed.
